wine.name: Scharzhofberger Riesling Spätlese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Spätlese: late picked, at least 76 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from old vines, some of them on their own roots.
wine.sites: The Scharzhofberg, the steep south facing hill of grey slate above the Scharzhof at Wiltingen, in the cold Saar valley; the estate farms its share from the house at its foot.
wine.making: The hill is picked in repeated selective passes, so that each Prädikat is a true selection. The grapes are pressed gently and the juice ferments slowly with the cellar's own yeasts, much of it in old oak Fuder casks, until the cold of the cellar stops it with natural sugar left behind. The wine rests on its lees through the winter and is bottled in spring.
wine.glass: White peach, apricot and lime blossom over wet slate and green apple; the sugar reads as texture rather than sweetness against a piercing Saar acidity, and age adds honey, quince and smoke.
wine.ageing: Delicious young for its fruit, it then closes for some years, and a strong vintage keeps for thirty years and more.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with crab, pork cooked with fruit, or on its own.

label.means: The vineyard, an Ortsteil, printed without the village name Wiltingen.
Late picked, at least 76 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel; here naturally sweet.
The wine region, named Mosel-Saar-Ruwer until 2007; the Saar lies within it.

records.table: Egon Müller's Scharzhofberger Riesling Spätlese comes from the steep grey slate hill above the Scharzhof in the cold Saar valley. It is low in alcohol and naturally sweet, peach and apricot over slate, with an acidity so high that the sugar reads as texture.
records.story: Through the Middle Ages the Scharzhof and its hill belonged to a monastery of Trier, and the slope above the house was planted with vines for centuries before any Müller lived there. When the French, who then held the left bank of the Rhine, took church property and sold it, the estate changed hands, and in 1797, by the house's account, it passed to the family whose descendants have kept it. Several heads of the house in the generations that followed carried the name Egon, so the label names a line rather than one man. Germany's wine law of 1971 fixed the Prädikat ladder of Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese that the labels follow, and the Saar became part of a region simply called Mosel in 2007. Through those changes the estate held to sweet wine of very low alcohol and very high acid, picking the hill in several passes so that each Prädikat is a true selection. Its rarer Auslesen and Trockenbeerenauslesen go to the September auction of the Grosser Ring at Trier, the association of the Mosel's auction estates founded in 1908. For a sommelier the Spätlese is the Saar's measure in the glass: the same hill and the same hand as the auction wines, in a frame a table can share.

wine.name: Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Auslese: selected bunches, at least 83 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, much of it from old vines.
wine.sites: The Wehlener Sonnenuhr, a steep slope of blue Devonian slate across the river from Wehlen, named for the sundial set in its rock in 1842.
wine.making: Bunches chosen for ripeness and noble rot are picked by hand in a late pass, pressed and fermented with the cellar's own yeasts, the fermentation stopped to leave natural sugar. The young wines keep a reductive, sulphurous smell and a faint prickle that the house is known for.
wine.glass: In youth struck match and smoke over white peach and lime, with a faint prickle; with age honey, candied apricot, quince and slate, sweet yet weightless and lifted by bright acidity.
wine.ageing: Often unapproachable for years, it opens after ten and keeps for several decades, turning to honey and smoke.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly so the struck match can clear; a white wine glass.

label.means: The sundial vineyard of Wehlen; the village comes first, with er added.

records.table: JJ Prüm's Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese comes from the blue slate slope across the river from Wehlen, named for its sundial. Young it smells of struck match and needs years; with age it turns to honey and smoke while staying light.
records.story: The sundial that names the Sonnenuhr was set in the slate across the river from Wehlen in 1842 by a member of the Prüm family, so that the people working the steep slope could tell the time. The family's holdings were divided among heirs in 1911, and the son who took his share founded the estate whose label carries his name in short. His own son ran it from the 1920s to the 1960s and gave it the style it is known by: picking late, fermenting with the cellar's own yeasts and stopping with natural sugar, so that the young wines smell of struck match and seem closed for years. Germany's wine law of 1971 set the Prädikat names on the labels, and the house used the colour of the capsule to mark finer selections within them, a gold capsule for a richer Auslese and a long gold capsule richer again. Other Prüm estates share the name and the village, which keeps guests and candidates alert. The estate's fame rests on sweet wines that a patient cellar turns into honey and smoke over decades. For a sommelier the Auslese teaches two habits at once: read the village before the vineyard, and look at the capsule as well as the print.

wine.name: Erdener Prälat Riesling Auslese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein: Auslese, the selected harvest, 83 degrees Oechsle at least on the Mosel
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from old vines on their own roots.
wine.sites: The Prälat, a tiny amphitheatre of red slate between the cliffs and the river at Erden, counted the warmest site of the Mittelmosel; the rock stores the sun and the water reflects it.
wine.making: Picked late by hand, often with some noble rot, the grapes are pressed gently and the juice ferments slowly in the traditional old Fuder casks of the estate's cellar. The fermentation stops with natural sugar left behind, and the wine rests on its lees before bottling.
wine.glass: Ripe apricot, mango and blood orange over smoke, ginger and red slate, with honey and saffron; rich and concentrated, yet carried by bright acidity to a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Rich enough to enjoy within five years, it gains depth for twenty and keeps for decades.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass and a modest pour, with blue cheese or a fruit tart.

records.table: Dr. Loosen's Erdener Prälat Riesling Auslese comes from old ungrafted vines in a tiny red slate amphitheatre between cliff and river, counted the warmest site of the Mittelmosel. It is rich and sweet, apricot and blood orange over smoke and ginger, and bright.
records.story: The Loosen family has owned vineyards around Bernkastel for some two centuries, by its own account, and over that time it gathered parcels in the great slopes downriver: the Würzgarten at Ürzig and the Treppchen and the Prälat at Erden. The Prälat takes its name from a prelate, a churchman who once held it, and its red slate between cliffs and water makes it the warm heart of that stretch of the river. Many of the family's vines there grow on their own roots, phylloxera having been ill at home in the dry slate. In 1988 a son of the family took over the estate and set it on a new course: lower yields, long ageing in the old Fuder casks of the cellar, and a campaign to carry Mosel Riesling back onto the wine lists of the world. That work took the estate beyond the valley. In 1999 it made the first Eroica Riesling with Chateau Ste. Michelle of Washington State, and it also took on an estate in the Pfalz. The Prälat Auslese stayed at the centre of the range as the estate's most concentrated wine. Set beside a Wehlen wine, it shows a sommelier the other face of the slate: red rock and warmth, orange and ginger where blue slate gives peach and lime.

wine.name: Bernkasteler Doctor Riesling Spätlese
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, the Spätlese rung: grapes picked late, 76 degrees Oechsle at least here
wine.sites: The Bernkasteler Doctor, a small, near vertical slope of grey slate directly behind the town of Bernkastel, its soil richer in clay and loam than the blue slate upriver.
wine.making: Picked by hand in selective passes, the grapes are pressed gently and the juice ferments cool; the fermentation is stopped to keep natural sweetness, and the wine rests on its lees before it is bottled in the spring after the harvest.
wine.glass: Smoke and apple skin over white peach, lemon and grey slate; dense and upright, with the Doctor's weight behind a firm acidity and a sweetness that reads lighter than it is.
wine.ageing: Firm and closed for five years or more, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty and longer in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, with smoked trout or roast pork.

records.table: Thanisch's Bernkasteler Doctor Riesling Spätlese, from the heirs' estate at Bernkastel, comes from the steep grey slate slope right behind the town, named, the legend says, for an archbishop it cured. It is smoky and dense, apple and peach, sweet but upright.
records.story: The legend of the Doctor is set in 1360: an Archbishop of Trier, lying ill with a fever at the castle above Bernkastel, was brought wine from this slope and recovered, and he named it the true doctor. The vineyard has carried the name since. The Thanisch family, at Bernkastel for centuries by its own account, came to hold a large share of the slope in the nineteenth century. When the head of the family, a doctor by degree, died towards the end of that century, his widow took charge, and her title stayed on the label: Wwe., short for Witwe, before Dr. H. Thanisch. Through the twentieth century the Doctor was shared among only a few owners, and Germany's wine law of 1971 set the Prädikat names, Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese, that its labels carry. Later the family divided its holdings between heirs, and two estates came to bear the name, Erben Thanisch and Erben Müller-Burggraef, each with its own part of the Doctor. The Spätlese is the house's classic reading of the site: smoky, dense and firm, where Wehlen is lighter and Graach broader. For a sommelier the long name is the lesson: read it to the end, since the heirs, not the widow, tell you which house made the wine.

wine.name: Maximin Grünhäuser Abtsberg Riesling Kabinett
wine.classification: Prädikatswein, Kabinett: the lightest rung, at least 70 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel
wine.sites: The Abtsberg, the abbot's hill, the first in rank of the estate's three walled slopes above the manor house at Mertesdorf in the Ruwer valley, on slate.
wine.making: Picked by hand and pressed gently, the grapes ferment with the cellar's own yeasts in the vaulted cellar below the house, and the fermentation is stopped to keep a gentle natural sweetness. The wine rests on its lees and is bottled in the spring.
wine.glass: Green apple, lime and blackcurrant leaf over wet slate, with a hint of white peach; feather light, racy and long, its gentle sweetness reading almost dry against the Ruwer's acidity.
wine.ageing: Bright and charming young, a good Abtsberg Kabinett keeps and gains for ten to twenty years.
wine.serve: 7 to 9 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, as an aperitif or with river trout.

label.means: The estate's name standing in place of a village, as an Ortsteil does, before each vineyard.
The abbot's hill, first in rank of the three, above Herrenberg and Bruderberg.
The lightest Prädikat, at least 70 degrees Oechsle on the Mosel; here gently sweet.

records.table: Maximin Grünhaus's Abtsberg Riesling Kabinett comes from the abbot's hill of an old Benedictine estate in the Ruwer valley, bought by the von Schubert family in 1882. It is feather light, green apple and blackcurrant leaf over slate, and tastes nearly dry.
records.story: The Grünhaus first appears in the records in 966, when the Emperor Otto I (912 to 973) confirmed it as a possession of the Benedictine abbey of St Maximin at Trier, and the abbey's monks worked its slopes for some eight centuries. The order of its three walled vineyards follows the abbey's own ranks: the Abtsberg was the abbot's, the Herrenberg the lords', the Bruderberg the brothers'. Under French rule at the start of the nineteenth century the abbey's lands were taken and sold, and in 1882 the estate was bought by the von Schubert family. They kept the three vineyards apart and printed each name under the estate's own, Maximin Grünhäuser, which German law treats as an Ortsteil standing in place of a village. The Ruwer is a small, cool side valley, and its wines are among the region's most delicate, scented with herbs and blackcurrant leaf. When the region's name was shortened to Mosel in 2007, the Ruwer's name left the label, though the valley's style did not. The Abtsberg is the estate's first wine in rank, and its Kabinett is the lightest way to meet it. For a sommelier the three names teach in one breath how an abbey ranked its own hills.

traps: Abtsberg, Herrenberg and Bruderberg are three vineyards of one estate, ranked as the abbey ranked its people: abbot, lords, brothers.
Maximin Grünhaus lies on the Ruwer, a side valley within the Mosel region, not on the Saar.
Maximin Grünhäuser stands in place of a village name, as an Ortsteil does, so no village appears on the label.

No page or search was open to this run (the shared search budget was spent before chunk f4 began and the network refuses every host), so the record rests on the Codex's Mosel record (the former Benedictine estate at Mertesdorf on the Ruwer, the three walled sites and their ranks, the Ortsteil label, the Ruwer's herbs and blackcurrant leaf), the Codex's advanced bank (the estate on the Ruwer, a one estate classification), the plan's 966 and 1882, and the author's knowledge of the Oxford Companion and the World Atlas, neither opened here.
The dates 966 and 1882 still need two sources or the estate's own history page: the refuter should confirm them first, with the Emperor's confirmation of 966 and the sale under French rule.
founded is empty: 966 is the first record, not a founding, and 1882 a purchase, so neither is given as the founding year.

The soils of the three hills (the author recalls blue slate for the Abtsberg and red for the Herrenberg), their aspects and the cellar's vessels are left out or given as slate alone, for want of a source.
The family's living members are not named; the record says only that the von Schubert family bought the estate in 1882, as history.
The plan names no Prädikat for this house; Kabinett is taught as the lightest reading of the Abtsberg and the one Kabinett of the group.
